facts.quote: The structure is eight stories high on the Pennsylvania Avenue NW side, and 11 stories high on the E Street NW side. Two wings connect the two main buildings, forming an open-air, trapezoidal courtyard.

facts.fact: The outside is buff precast and cast-in-place concrete with repeated square bronze-tinted windows set deep in concrete frames.
facts.quote: The exterior is buff-colored precast and cast-in-place concrete with repetitive, square, bronze-tinted windows set deep in concrete frames.

facts.fact: The building is Brutalist, and its concrete still shows the marks of the rough wood forms it was poured into.
facts.quote: The J. Edgar Hoover Building is in an architectural style known as Brutalism. The term is derived from the French term béton brut ("raw concrete"); in Brutalist structures, unprocessed concrete surfaces are commonly used to create "rugged, dramatic surfaces and monumental sculptural forms." The concrete of the Hoover Building shows the marks from the rough wood forms into which the liquid concrete was poured.

facts.fact: The FBI wanted a building that was bomb-proof on its lower floors with only a few tightly secured entrances.
facts.quote: But the FBI rejected this view, instead advocating a structure which was bomb-proof on the first few stories and which had but a few, tightly secured access points elsewhere.

facts.fact: Reactions ranged from strong praise to strong disapproval when it opened; more recently it has been widely condemned on aesthetic and urban planning grounds.
facts.quote: Critical reaction to the J. Edgar Hoover Building ranged from strong praise to strong disapproval when it opened. More recently, it has been widely condemned on aesthetic and urban planning grounds.

facts.fact: Paul Rudolph designed the Temple Street Parking Garage in New Haven in 1961, after his time leading Yale's architecture department.
facts.quote: Rudolph stayed at Yale for six years until he returned to private practice. He designed the Temple Street Parking Garage, also in New Haven, in 1961.

facts.fact: Wurster Hall was completed on the Berkeley campus in 1964, designed by faculty members Joseph Esherick, Vernon DeMars and Donald Olsen.
facts.quote: Bauer Wurster Hall was completed in 1964 on the Berkeley campus, designed by faculty members Joseph Esherick, Vernon DeMars, and Donald Olsen; Bauer Wurster Hall, in which the college is housed, is named in his and his wife's honor.

facts.fact: It was built to house the new College of Environmental Design and was renamed Bauer Wurster Hall in 2020 to honour both William Wurster and Catherine Bauer Wurster.
facts.quote: Wurster Hall, designed by  CED faculty Joseph Esherick, Vernon DeMars, and Donald Olsen to house the new college, opened in 1964; the building was renamed Bauer Wurster Hall in 2020 after archival documentation came to light revealing that the building name was intended to recognize both William W. Wurster and Catherine Bauer Wurster, associate dean of the college, for their contributions to the founding of CED.

facts.fact: The college was founded in 1959, when William Wurster brought architecture, landscape architecture, city planning and decorative arts together.
facts.quote: The College of Environmental Design was founded in 1959, when Dean William W. Wurster brought together four existing campus units to create a multidisciplinary approach to the built environment: the School of Architecture (founded 1903 by John Galen Howard), the School of Landscape Architecture (founded 1913 by John William Gregg), the Department of City Planning (founded 1948), and the Department of Decorative Arts.

facts.fact: The building stands at the southeast corner of the main UC Berkeley campus.
facts.quote: The college is housed in Bauer Wurster Hall at the southeast corner of the main UC Berkeley campus.

facts.fact: Berkeley's architecture school, founded in 1903, was the first in the western United States.
facts.quote: This was the first architecture school to be established in the western United States and only the seventh in the nation.

facts.fact: The Institute for Hygiene and Microbiology stands close to the Mouse Bunker and the Benjamin Franklin Medical Center; the three were built as infrastructure for developing new medicines and vaccines.
facts.quote: It is located in close proximity to the Benjamin Franklin Medical Center and the Institute for Hygiene and Microbiology. These three facilities were erected to provide a high performing infrastructure for the development and application of new medicine and vaccines.

facts.fact: The documentary Battleship Berlin covers the institute together with its neighbour, the Mouse Bunker.
facts.quote: Filmmaker Nathan Eddy shot the documentary Battleship Berlin, which deals with the Research Institutes for Experimental Medicine and the neighboring Institute for Hygiene and Microbiology.

facts.fact: St Agnes in Kreuzberg is a former Catholic church complex built in the 1960s by Werner Düttmann, considered a prime example of Brutalism; König Galerie moved in in May 2015.
facts.quote: In May 2015, König Galerie took up a second location at St Agnes in Kreuzberg, a former Catholic church complex that was built in the 1960s by the German architect and city planner Werner Düttmann and considered to be a prime example of Brutalism.

facts.fact: It gives the gallery 800 square metres of exhibition space.
facts.quote: It provides an exhibition space of 800 m2 (8,600 sq ft).

facts.fact: Johann König took a long-term lease in 2012, and Arno Brandlhuber converted the complex into an exhibition space.
facts.quote: In 2012, König signed a long-term lease for the complex, and it was converted by the German architect Arno Brandlhuber into an exhibition space for his gallery.

facts.fact: The conversion won the Berlin Architectural Prize 2016.
facts.quote: The project, commissioned by Johann and Lena König, won the Berlin Architectural Prize 2016.

facts.fact: The building also houses other tenants, including New York University Berlin's art studio.
facts.quote: Today, the building also accommodates other tenants, including New York University Berlin’s art studio.

facts.fact: The Eastern City Gate, officially named Rudo, is a complex of three large residential buildings by the E-75 motorway, finished in 1976 and seen as a symbol of Belgrade and of Yugoslav socialism.
facts.quote: The complex, which is officially named Rudo, was finished in 1976 and is considered one of the symbols of the city, and of the Yugoslav Socialism in general.

facts.fact: It was built from 1973 to 1976, designed by architect Vera Ćirković and civil engineer Milutin Jerotijević, with urban design by Milica Jakšić.
facts.quote: Eastern Gate was constructed from 1973 to 1976. The buildings were designed by architect Vera Ćirković and civil engineer Milutin Jerotijević. The urban design of the complex was drafted by Milica Jakšić.

facts.fact: Each of the three buildings has 28 storeys and 190 apartments and is 85 metres tall.
facts.quote: The complex consists of three buildings and each of them has 28 storeys and 190 apartments. They are 85 m (279 ft) tall each.

facts.fact: Like the Western City Gate, it was built in the brutalist style.
facts.quote: Just like its western counterpart, the Western City Gate, it was built in the brutalist style.

facts.fact: The three stepped, triangular buildings stand in a circle, so one always seems to sit between the other two.
facts.quote: All three buildings are step-like and triangular shaped, built in a circle so it always visually appears that one is between the other two.

facts.fact: The site supervisor, Dragoljub Mićović, named the buildings after his hometown of Rudo.
facts.quote: Dragoljub Mićović performed professional supervision during the construction, who also named them after his hometown of Rudo.

facts.fact: By 2013 concrete chunks of up to 60 kg were falling from the facade, which experts described as in extremely bad shape.
facts.quote: By 2013, concrete chunks up to 60 kg (130 lb) began to fall off the buildings. Experts from the University of Belgrade Faculty of Civil Engineering described the facade as being in "extremely bad shape".

facts.fact: Ruhr University Bochum was founded in 1962 as Germany's first new public university after the Second World War, and teaching began in 1965.
facts.quote: It was founded in 1962 as the first new public university in Germany after World War II. Instruction began in 1965.

facts.fact: Unlike many older German universities, all its buildings stand on one campus south of the city.
facts.quote: Unlike many older German universities, the buildings of Ruhr-University are all centralized on one campus, located south of Bochum city.

facts.fact: The campus is almost entirely 1960s brutalism, made up of 14 almost identical high-rise buildings.
facts.quote: The centralized university campus architecture is comprised almost exclusively of the 1960s architecture style referred to as brutalism, consisting of 14 almost identical high-rise buildings.

facts.fact: The roofs all appear to sit at the same level, while the buildings' real heights vary with the rolling ground on high land beside the Ruhr valley.
facts.quote: One striking feature of these buildings is that although their roofs are all at the same apparent height (sky level), the absolute heights of the buildings vary in accordance with their placement on the undulating landscape in which the university is located: the campus is at the edge of a green belt on high ground adjacent to the Ruhr valley.

facts.fact: Helmut Hentrich's office did the overall planning and an institute building for the university between 1963 and 1972.
facts.quote: 1963–1972: Overall planning and institute building of the Ruhr University Bochum.

facts.fact: Some of the original 1960s buildings are being rebuilt rather than refurbished because of PCB contamination.
facts.quote: Some of the original 1960s buildings are to be rebuilt, instead of refurbished, due to PCB contamination.

facts.fact: Georgi Konstantinovski won first prize in the 1969 competition for the Goce Delčev student dormitory in Skopje.
facts.quote: 1969 – 1st prize, Students' Dormitory "Goce Delcev", Skopje

facts.fact: The dormitory received a Borba plaquette award in 1972.
facts.quote: 1972 – Borba plaquette for the Students' Dormitory "Goce Delcev", Skopje

facts.fact: The dormitories are among Konstantinovski's best-known buildings.
facts.quote: Some of his most renowned buildings are the City Archive in Skopje, the Student's Dormitories "Goce Delcev", the Institute of Earthquake Engineering and Engineering Seismology, the ASNOM Memorial Center, and the Memorial House of Razlovci Uprising.

facts.fact: TASS is headquartered in a Soviet brutalist building built in 1977.
facts.quote: TASS is headquartered in a building in the Soviet brutalist style built in 1977.

facts.fact: In 2021 Russian architects criticised Moscow's plans to renovate the building without care for its historic appearance.
facts.quote: In November 2021, an association of Russian architects criticized plans by Moscow city authorities to renovate the building without due regard for the preservation of its historic appearance.

facts.fact: The Queensland Art Gallery opened in 1982 as the first stage of Robin Gibson's Queensland Cultural Centre on Brisbane's South Bank.
facts.quote: The first stage of the monumental Robin Gibson-designed Queensland Cultural Centre opened on Brisbane's South Bank in 1982.

facts.fact: It was the first major building on the south side of the river beside the new Victoria Bridge, setting a benchmark of scale and quality for later buildings.
facts.quote: It was also the first major building to be built on the south side of the river adjacent to the new Victoria Bridge, which established a benchmark of scale and quality for future buildings.

facts.fact: The Watermall is the main orientation element, separating the quiet exhibition galleries from administration, public programmes and education areas.
facts.quote: The primary orientation element of the Gallery's design is the Watermall that separates the tranquil environment of the exhibition galleries from the proactive environments of the administration, public programs and education areas.

facts.fact: Varying ceiling heights, floor levels, colours and textures define the sequence of display areas.
facts.quote: The varying ceilings heights and floor levels, colour and textured surfaces enhance variety and define the sequence of display areas.

facts.fact: Light-coloured, maintenance-free materials such as cement respond to Brisbane's subtropical climate.
facts.quote: The buildings use of light coloured and maintenance free materials such as cement reflect and adapt to the Mediterranean- like quality of Brisbane's sub tropical climate.

facts.fact: It has 4,700 square metres of display space, with walls placed to steer the visitor's route.
facts.quote: The Queensland Art Gallery is a 4700 square metre display space broken down with walls and barriers that interchange between the art world and the public. The walls have been placed purposely to create flow and change of course of the viewer's journey.

facts.fact: In 2004 it received the Queensland architects' 25 Year Award, now the Robin Gibson Award for Enduring Architecture.
facts.quote: In 2004 the Queensland Art Gallery (completed in 1982) was awarded the '25 Year Award', now known as the Robin Gibson Award for Enduring Architecture by the Queensland Chapter of the Australian Institute of Architects.

facts.fact: The gallery was listed as a State Heritage Place in 2015.
facts.quote: The Queensland Art Gallery was listed as a State Heritage Place in 2015.

facts.fact: The Golden Mile Complex is a high-rise commercial and residential building on Beach Road in Singapore.
facts.quote: The Golden Mile, formerly Golden Mile Complex (Chinese: 黄金坊; pinyin: Huángjīn fāng), is a high-rise commercial and residential building on Beach Road in Kallang, Singapore.

facts.fact: It was designed by Gan Eng Oon, William Lim and Tay Kheng Soon of Design Partnership (now DP Architects).
facts.quote: The building was designed by Gan Eng Oon, William Lim and Tay Kheng Soon of the Singapore architect firm Design Partnership, now known as DP Architects.

facts.fact: Completed in 1973 for S$18 million, the 16-storey building was an early pioneer of mixed-use development in Singapore.
facts.quote: Built at a cost of S$18 million and completed in 1973, the 16-storey Golden Mile Complex is one of the early pioneers of integrating multiple operations into a single mixed-use development in Singapore.

facts.fact: It is an example of the 'megastructure' described by Reyner Banham, one of few actually built; Fumihiko Maki called it a 'collective form'.
facts.quote: Sited on 1.3 hectares and built to a height of 89 metres, the Golden Mile Complex is an exemplary type of "megastructure" described by architectural historian, Reyner Banham. It is one of the few that have been actually realised in the world. Pritzker Architecture Prize laureate Fumihiko Maki had called the Golden Mile Complex a "collective form".

facts.fact: The design drew on the linear city ideas of Le Corbusier and Arturo Soria y Mata.
facts.quote: The design was influenced by the linear city concepts of Le Corbusier and Arturo Soria y Mata.

facts.fact: The stepped terraces give upper-floor flats sea views, and the narrow sloping slab helps natural ventilation and shades a high communal concourse over the podium.
facts.quote: The step-terraced profile of the Golden Mile Complex offers the occupants of the apartments on the upper floors panoramic view of the sea and sky. Every apartment has its own balcony. The crown houses two-storey maisonette penthouses. The narrowness of this sloping slab form enhances natural ventilation and shades a lofty communal concourse above the podium along Beach Road.

facts.fact: Offices and a shopping mall fill the lower floors, set in staggered atria that bring daylight into the building.
facts.quote: The lower floors contain offices and a retail mall, located within staggered atria to allow natural light into the heart of the building.

facts.fact: The government announced it would be conserved in October 2021.
facts.quote: On 22 October 2021, the Minister for National Development Desmond Lee announced the gazetting of the Golden Mile Complex as a conserved building.

facts.fact: The Joseph Regenstein Library is the main library of the University of Chicago and is noted for its brutalist architecture.
facts.quote: Named after the industrialist and philanthropist Joseph Regenstein, it is one of the largest repositories of books in the world. The Regenstein is noted for its brutalist architecture.

facts.fact: It stands on the former grounds of Stagg Field.
facts.quote: The library stands on the former grounds of Stagg Field.

facts.fact: Ground was broken in 1968 and the library opened in 1970 at a final cost of $20,750,000.
facts.quote: In 1968, the university broke ground, and in 1970 the library opened at the final cost of $20,750,000.

facts.fact: Skidmore, Owings & Merrill designed it, led by Walter Netsch, in grooved limestone that looks like concrete from a distance.
facts.quote: The building was designed by the Chicago firm Skidmore, Owings & Merrill, led by senior architect Walter Netsch. It is built out of grooved limestone, which, from a distance, resembles concrete.

facts.fact: It has five floors above ground and two basements, each floor with a large central reading room.
facts.quote: The building has five floors above ground and two basements. Each floor has a large reading room in the center with desks, group study rooms, lockers and shelved reference works.

facts.fact: The reading rooms are kept apart from the stacks on the west side so the stacks can be held cooler for book conservation, and 220 faculty studies line the east side.
facts.quote: The reading rooms are separated from the stacks, located on the west side of the building, so that the stacks can be maintained at lower temperatures, which are more amicable to book conservation. Two hundred and twenty faculty studies line the east side of the building.

facts.fact: Helmut Jahn's glass-domed Mansueto Library, with automated storage underground, was added in 2011.
facts.quote: The Joe and Rika Mansueto Library, designed by Chicago-based architect Helmut Jahn, consists of a glass-domed reading room, under which lies an automated storage and retrieval system stretching fifty feet underground.

facts.fact: The Andrews Building, made of the Science and Humanities Wings, is the oldest structure on the University of Toronto's Scarborough campus.
facts.quote: The Science Wing (S-Wing) and Humanities Wing (H-Wing), known together as the Andrews Building, is an academic building of the University of Toronto and the oldest structure on its Scarborough campus in Toronto, Ontario, Canada.

facts.fact: The brutalist building was completed in 1964 and was one of John Andrews's first major commissions, at age 29.
facts.quote: The megalithic brutalist structure was built in 1964, near Highland Creek in the Toronto district of Scarborough. The Andrews Building is noted for its unique architecture, described as futuristic and forward-thinking for its time. It was one of the first major commissions of architect and professor John Andrews at the age of 29, who later went on to help design the CN Tower.

facts.fact: When built it was one of the largest mainly concrete buildings in the world.
facts.quote: At the time of its construction, it was one of the largest predominantly concrete buildings in the world.

facts.fact: Andrews laid it out as 'indoor streets' to shield students from the winter cold.
facts.quote: The large building's unconventional layout was designed by John Andrews to act as "indoor streets," to reduce the need for outdoor travel and shield students from the cold during winter months.

facts.fact: The two wings meet at a central atrium, the Meeting Place, under a large coffered concrete skylight; outside, a stepped concrete pinnacle rises to three large chimneys.
facts.quote: Its two wings, the Humanities and Science wings, are connected by a central atrium known as the Meeting Place, set below a large concrete coffered skylight. The building's exterior features a prominent stepped concrete pinnacle rising from the main structure's sloped walls, topped by three large chimneys.

facts.fact: It was designed for distance learning, with lectures recorded downtown and played to students through a television system.
facts.quote: The building was designed with the intention of conducting distance learning through an extensive television system. Lectures were to be recorded at St. George and played for students at Scarborough College to eliminate the need for travel between the two campuses.

facts.fact: Andrews objected to the label 'brutalist', calling Scarborough College a very human building.
facts.quote: John Andrews disliked the term "brutalist" due to its negative connotation; he is quoted as saying “I object quite strongly to the word ‘brutalist’, continuing that “It isn’t brutal. Scarborough College is a very human building.”

facts.fact: It was on the cover of Time magazine in January 1967.
facts.quote: The building was featured on the cover of Time magazine in its January 13, 1967 issue.

facts.fact: Completed in 1963 on Virginia Key, it was the first stadium in the United States built for powerboat racing.
facts.quote: The facility, completed in 1963 on land donated to the City of Miami from the Matheson family, is the first stadium purpose-built for powerboat racing in the United States.

facts.fact: The 6,566-seat stadium was designed by Hilario Candela, then a 28-year-old recent immigrant from Cuba.
facts.quote: The structure was built on land donated for water sports, and designed by architect Hilario Candela, then a 28-year-old recent immigrant from Cuba.

facts.fact: Poured entirely in concrete, it has a cantilevered folded-plate roof held by eight large slanted columns anchored through the grandstand.
facts.quote: Poured entirely in concrete, the Miami Marine Stadium consists of a cantilevered folded plate roof supported by eight large slanted columns anchored in the ground through the grandstand. A huge horizontal beam tied them all together.

facts.fact: The columns were pushed as far back as possible so spectators had clear views over the water.
facts.quote: A cut in the seating arrangement allowed spectators to appreciate the full height of the posts, which were pushed as far back as possible to permit unobstructed views over the watercourse.

facts.fact: Candela's design was shaped by his work at a Cuban firm collaborating with Félix Candela and by internships with Max Borges Jr., architect of the Tropicana Club.
facts.quote: During this period, the firm was working with Spanish-born architect Félix Candela, a distant relative of Hilario, on the Bacardí warehouse in Mexico. This experience – coupled with previous summer internships in the office of Max Borges Jr., the architect of the famed Tropicana Club in Havana – ultimately influenced his approach to designing the Marine Stadium for which he is best known.

facts.fact: It was declared unsafe and abandoned in 1992 after Hurricane Andrew, and listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2018.
facts.quote: The stadium was abandoned in 1992 when officials declared it unsafe following Hurricane Andrew. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2018.

facts.fact: The National Trust for Historic Preservation named it one of America's 11 Most Endangered Historic Places in 2009 and a National Treasure in 2012.
facts.quote: In 2009, the National Trust for Historic Preservation named the Commodore Ralph Middleton Munroe Marine Stadium to its list of America's 11 Most Endangered Historic Places. The National Trust designated the stadium as a National Treasure in March 2012.

facts.fact: In Bratislava the Slovak National Gallery is housed in the adjacent Esterházy Palace and Water Barracks.
facts.quote: In Bratislava, it has its displays situated in Esterházy Palace (Esterházyho palác) and the Water Barracks (Vodné kasárne) which are adjacent to each other.

facts.fact: The Esterházy Palace was rebuilt for the gallery in the 1950s, and a modern extension was added in the 1970s.
facts.quote: The Esterházy Palace was reconstructed for the purposes of the gallery in the 1950s and a modern extension was added in the 1970s.

facts.fact: University Hall was designed by Arthur Erickson and sits in the coulees above the Oldman River.
facts.quote: University Hall was designed by the renowned architect Arthur Erickson and sits within the coulees above the Oldman River.

facts.fact: Its completion in 1971 let the university move permanently to west Lethbridge.
facts.quote: With the completion of University Hall in 1971, the university moved permanently to west Lethbridge with enrolment growing to over 1,200 students.

facts.fact: The west Lethbridge site was chosen after a community debate and a protest march in 1968.
facts.quote: After the university's first convocation on May 18, 1968, more than 500 students, faculty and community members held a protest march in support of having the university located in west Lethbridge. Soon after, the government decided west Lethbridge would be the university's permanent location.

facts.fact: It was one of four buildings on a Canadian stamp marking the 100th anniversary of the Royal Architectural Institute of Canada.
facts.quote: University Hall was selected as one of four buildings to appear on a Canadian postage stamp celebrating the 100th anniversary of the Royal Architectural Institute of Canada (RAIC).

facts.fact: The National Arts Centre is Canada's performing arts centre in Ottawa, beside the Rideau Canal, and a National Historic Site since 2006.
facts.quote: The National Arts Centre (NAC) (French: Centre national des Arts) is a Canadian centre for the performing arts located in Ottawa, Ontario, along the Rideau Canal. It is operated by the eponymous performing arts organisation National Arts Centre. The National Arts Centre was designated a National Historic Site of Canada in 2006.

facts.fact: It was one of the projects for Canada's 1967 centenary and opened on 31 May 1969.
facts.quote: The NAC was one of a number of projects launched by the government of Lester B. Pearson to commemorate Canada's 1967 centenary. It opened its doors to the public for the first time on May 31, 1969, at a cost of C$46 million.

facts.fact: Fred Lebensold designed it in the Brutalist style in reinforced concrete, based on the triangle and hexagon.
facts.quote: The building, designed by Fred Lebensold, is in the Brutalist style and is based on the shape of a triangle and hexagon. The building is constructed of reinforced concrete.

facts.fact: Walls are faced with precast concrete panels with exposed crushed brown Laurentian granite.
facts.quote: The exterior and many interior walls are faced with precast concrete panels containing exposed aggregate of crushed brown Laurentian granite.

facts.fact: The roof of the base is a multi-level public terrace with gardens, and the three main halls rise from it as hexagonal volumes.
facts.quote: The roof of the base forms a multi-level terrace containing gardens that are open to the public and connects to the Mackenzie King Bridge. The three main performance spaces rise from the base as a series of hexagonal structures also faced with brown precast panels in a variety of textures.

facts.fact: The hexagon theme continues inside, in ceilings, light fittings and floors.
facts.quote: The hexagonal theme flows through the interior and appears in ceilings, light fixtures and flooring.

facts.fact: A renovation reoriented the centre towards Parliament Hill and reopened on 1 July 2017.
facts.quote: The work would expand meeting and event facilities, install entrances and windows to reorient the focus toward Parliament Hill, and upgrade washroom facilities. The renovated centre opened on July 1, 2017 for Canada's 150th Anniversary.

facts.fact: In 1969, on the 25th anniversary of the camp's liberation, a monument to the victims was put up at Majdanek, designed by sculptor and architect Wiktor Tołkin.
facts.quote: In 1969, on the 25th anniversary of the Majdanek liberation, a monument dedicated to Holocaust victims was erected on the grounds of the former Nazi extermination camp. It was designed by a Polish sculptor and architect Wiktor Tołkin, who also designed the symbolic tombstone at Stutthof.

facts.fact: The monument has three parts: an 11-metre-tall, 35-metre-wide gate called the Pylon, the road, and the Mausoleum holding a mound of the victims' ashes.
facts.quote: The monument consists of three parts, the symbolic Pylon (gate, 11 meters tall and 35 meters wide), the road, and the Mausoleum, containing a mound of ashes of the victims.

facts.fact: The gate stands at the camp entrance and the mausoleum at the opposite end.
facts.quote: It consists of two parts: a large gate monument at the camp's entrance and a large mausoleum holding ashes of the victims at its opposite end.

facts.fact: In 1947 about 1,300 cubic metres of soil mixed with human ashes and bone fragments were gathered into a mound, later turned into the mausoleum.
facts.quote: In the same year, some 1,300 m3 of surface soil mixed with human ashes and fragments of bones were collected and arranged into a large mound (since turned into a mausoleum).

facts.fact: The site's museum, founded in autumn 1944, was the first museum in the world devoted to the crimes of the Nazi camps.
facts.quote: It was the first museum of its kind in the world, devoted entirely to the memory of atrocities committed in the network of concentration, slave-labor, and extermination camps and subcamps of KL Lublin during World War II.

facts.fact: The National Museum of Modern Art, Kyoto (MoMAK) is an art museum in Kyoto.
facts.quote: The National Museum of Modern Art, Kyoto (京都国立近代美術館, Kyōto Kokuritsu Kindai Bijutsukan) is an art museum in Kyoto, Japan.

facts.fact: The museum's old building was taken down and replaced by the present building designed by Fumihiko Maki.
facts.quote: Seventeen years later, the old building was dismantled and the present building, designed by  Fumihiko Maki was completed.

facts.fact: It opened on 26 October 1986 with about 9,762 m² of floor area, of which about 2,605 m² is exhibition space.
facts.quote: The museum was opened to the public on October 26, 1986, with 9,761.99 m² total floor area and 2,604.94 m² exhibition area.

facts.fact: It collects twentieth-century art from Japan and elsewhere, with an emphasis on artists of Kyoto and the Kansai region.
facts.quote: MoMAK is a national institution devoted to the collection and preservation of artworks and related reference materials of the twentieth century in Japan and other parts of the world.  Particular *emphasis is placed on artists or artistic movements in Kyoto and the Kansai area (the western region of Japan), such as Japanese-style paintings of the Kyoto School.

facts.fact: London Bridge, opened in 1836, is the oldest railway station in London's fare zone 1 and one of the oldest in the world.
facts.quote: The main line station is the oldest railway station in London fare zone 1 and one of the oldest in the world, having opened in 1836.

facts.fact: Grimshaw redeveloped the station between 2009 and 2017, rebuilding every platform and adding two major street-level entrances.
facts.quote: The station was comprehensively redeveloped by Grimshaw Architects between 2009 and 2017 with the rebuilding of all platforms, the addition of two major new street-level entrances, and changes to passenger concourses and retail facilities.

facts.fact: The 1970s footbridge was replaced by an interchange concourse under the platforms, reached by lift, stairs and escalator.
facts.quote: The footbridge dating from the 1970s that linked platforms for passenger interchange was also demolished, replaced by an interchange concourse underneath the platforms accessed by lift, stairs and escalator.

facts.fact: The platforms are linked by a large street-level concourse with entrances on St Thomas Street and Tooley Street.
facts.quote: The platforms are linked together by a large street-level concourse, offering a ticket office, retail facilities and waiting areas, with entrances on St Thomas Street and Tooley Street.

facts.fact: Through platforms went from six to nine, all long enough for 12-car trains.
facts.quote: Through platforms were increased from six to nine, all of which catered for 12-car trains.

facts.fact: Prince William opened the rebuilt station on 9 May 2018; the project was worth about £1 billion.
facts.quote: The refurbished station was officially opened by Prince William, Duke of Cambridge on 9 May 2018. The total estimated value of the project was around £1 billion.

facts.fact: The rebuilt station was shortlisted for the Stirling Prize in 2019.
facts.quote: In July 2019, the refurbished station made the shortlist for the Stirling Prize for excellence in architecture.

facts.fact: The redevelopment won the World Architecture Festival's transport category for completed buildings.
facts.quote: World Architecture Festival 'Transport- Completed Buildings' Category Winner—London Bridge station Redevelopment

facts.fact: Lanserhof Sylt is a 2022 project by ingenhoven associates.
facts.quote: 2022 Lanserhof Sylt

facts.fact: It won the 2023 MIPIM Award for best hospitality, leisure and tourism project.
facts.quote: 2023 MIPIM Awards, Best Hospitality, Leisure and Tourism for Lanserhof Sylt

facts.fact: It won the 2023 AHEAD Award for a new hotel building.
facts.quote: 2023 AHEAD Award Hotel Newbuild Lanserhof Sylt

facts.fact: It also won a World Architecture Festival award in 2023.
facts.quote: 2023 WAF Award for Lanserhof Sylt

facts.fact: The Nissay Theatre is in the Nissay Hibiya Building in Tokyo, designed by Togo Murano for Nippon Life's 70th anniversary.
facts.quote: It is located in the Nissay Hibiya Building, designed by the architect Togo Murano. It was constructed for the 70th anniversary of Nippon Life, a leading insurance company.

facts.fact: It was completed in 1963 and opened with the Japanese premiere of Beethoven's Fidelio by the Deutsche Oper Berlin.
facts.quote: The theatre was completed in 1963 and opened with the Japanese premiere of Beethoven's opera Fidelio by the Deutsche Oper Berlin.

facts.fact: Inside the 1,330-seat hall the walls and ceilings are curved, with no straight lines.
facts.quote: Inside the 1,330-seat theatre, the walls and ceilings are curved and there are no straight lines.

facts.fact: The ceiling is decorated with 20,000 pearl oyster shells.
facts.quote: The ceiling is decorated with 20,000 pearl oyster shells.

facts.fact: The theatre has staged kabuki, opera, musicals and family programmes.
facts.quote: Since then, a wide variety of performing arts shows have been staged at the theatre, including kabuki, operas, musicals, and family programs.

facts.fact: The Kadokawa Culture Museum, designed by Kengo Kuma, is a building holding several museums.
facts.quote: The Kadokawa Culture Museum is a multiple museum building designed by Kengo Kuma (famed for his Japan National Stadium, the host venue of the 2020 Summer Olympics in Tokyo).

facts.fact: It is part of Tokorozawa Sakura Town, a pop-culture complex by Kadokawa and the city of Tokorozawa that opened in autumn 2020.
facts.quote: Tokorozawa Sakura Town (Japanese: ところざわサクラタウン, Hepburn: Tokorozawa Sakura Taun) is a pop cultural attraction complex in Tokorozawa, Saitama, Japan which opened in the fall of 2020.  It is a joint project of the Kadokawa Corporation and the city of Tokorozawa.

facts.fact: An 8-metre, double-height library of more than 50,000 books turns into a 'bookshelf theatre' with projection mapping.
facts.quote: It features the permanent outdoor art installation "Resonating Life in the Acorn Forest" by TeamLab as well as a double-height 8-meter-tall (26 ft) library housing fifty thousand plus volumes which can morph into a 'bookshelf theater' via projection mapping.

facts.fact: The building is a monolith whose facade is clad in more than 20,000 granite pieces fitted to its many angled faces.
facts.quote: The museum structure is a monolith, the facade of which is clad in 20,000 plus granite pieces fitted to the multiple shifts within its obtuse shape.

facts.fact: Kuma said the design represents the Earth's energy breaking through the ground.
facts.quote: Kuma has said of the building's design that "It represents the Earth's energy that breaks through the ground".

facts.fact: Shinjuku Park Tower is the second-tallest building in Shinjuku.
facts.quote: The Shinjuku Park Tower (新宿パークタワー, Shinjuku Pāku Tawā) is the second-tallest building in Shinjuku, Tokyo.

facts.fact: It was designed by Kenzo Tange and completed in 1994.
facts.quote: It was designed by Kenzo Tange and completed in 1994.

facts.fact: It was built by Tokyo Gas's development arm on the site of a decommissioned gas storage facility.
facts.quote: The building is owned and managed by Tokyo Gas Urban Development, a subsidiary of Tokyo Gas, and was constructed on the site of a decommissioned gas storage facility.

facts.fact: A regional cooling centre on site heats and cools the Nishi-Shinjuku high-rise district and supplies electricity to the Tokyo Metropolitan Government Building.
facts.quote: Tokyo Gas operates a regional cooling center on-site, which provides heating and cooling to the high-rise district of Nishi-Shinjuku, and supplies electricity to the adjacent Tokyo Metropolitan Government Building.

facts.fact: It is one building of three connected blocks: 235 m with 52 storeys, 209 m with 47 storeys and 182 m with 41 storeys.
facts.quote: Shinjuku Park Tower is a single building consisting of three connected block-shaped elements; S tower, which is 235 m (771 ft) tall with 52 stories, C tower which is 209 m (686 ft) tall with 47 stories and N tower which is 182 m (597 ft) tall with 41 stories.

facts.fact: Shops fill floors 1 to 8, offices floors 9 to 37, and the Park Hyatt Tokyo hotel floors 39 to 52.
facts.quote: Floors 1 to 8 are occupied by retail stores, floors 9 to 37 are office floors and floors 39 to 52 are occupied by the luxury Park Hyatt Tokyo hotel, which includes a swimming pool with panoramic views on the city.

facts.fact: The Park Hyatt at the top was the main setting of Sofia Coppola's film Lost in Translation.
facts.quote: The Park Hyatt Tokyo hotel on the top was the main setting of the Sofia Coppola film Lost In Translation.

facts.fact: The Embassy of Kuwait is Kuwait's diplomatic mission in Japan; it faces Hijirizaka beside Mita Junior High School.
facts.quote: The Embassy of the State of Kuwait in Tokyo is the diplomatic mission of Kuwait in Japan. The embassy faces Hijirizaka and neighbours Mita Junior High School.

facts.fact: The current building was designed by Kenzo Tange and completed in 1970.
facts.quote: The current building was designed by Kenzo Tange and completed in 1970.

facts.fact: It is an example of both Brutalism and Metabolism.
facts.quote: It is an example of brutalism and metabolism.

facts.fact: It is one of Tange's few works built in Japan in the 1970s, when most of his work was abroad.
facts.quote: It is noted for being one of the few works by Tange in Japan built in the 1970s, as most of his works during this decade were built outside Japan.

facts.fact: The contractor was Kajima.
facts.quote: The contractor was Kajima.

facts.fact: Yoshinobu Ashihara designed the Komazawa Gymnasium together with the landmark Control Tower, the focal point of the park; the gymnasium hosted wrestling at the 1964 Olympics.
facts.quote: Designed by Japanese architect Yoshinobu Ashihara, along with the landmark Control Tower, that features as a focal point of the park, the gymnasium venue hosted the wrestling events at the 1964 Summer Olympics.

facts.fact: The gymnasium is an indoor arena in Komazawa Olympic Park seating 3,875.
facts.quote: Komazawa Gymnasium (駒沢オリンピック公園総合運動場体育館) is an indoor sporting arena located in Komazawa Olympic Park, Tokyo, Japan. The capacity of the arena is 3,875 spectators.

facts.fact: Toyota Stadium is a football stadium with a retractable roof in Toyota, Aichi, built in 2001.
facts.quote: Toyota Stadium (豊田スタジアム, Toyota Sutajiamu) is a stadium in Toyota, Aichi Prefecture, Japan. It has a retractable roof.

facts.fact: Kisho Kurokawa designed it between 1997 and 2001.
facts.quote: Toyota Stadium (Toyota City, 1997–2001)

facts.fact: Built in 2001, it is home to the J1 League club Nagoya Grampus and is designed for football only.
facts.quote: It was built in 2001 and is often used as home to the J1 League club Nagoya Grampus. The stadium is football-specific, which gives matches an authentic football aura; however, its location outside Nagoya city makes it impractical for consolidating the club's fan base in its billed hometown.

facts.fact: Its roof folds like an accordion, but it has not been closed since 2015 because of maintenance costs.
facts.quote: Its roof is unique in that it folds much like an accordion; however, the roof has never been closed since 2015 due to extra costs for maintenance.

facts.fact: It was a venue for the 2019 Rugby World Cup, the first held in Asia.
facts.quote: The stadium was also used as one of the venues for 2019 Rugby World Cup, the first Rugby World Cup to be held in Asia.

facts.fact: The NOA Building is a landmark 15-storey building in Tokyo's Azabu district, designed by Seiichi Shirai and built in 1974.
facts.quote: The NOA building is a landmark 15-storey building located in Tokyo’s Azabu district in Minato, Tokyo, Japan. Designed by Japanese architect Seiichi Shirai, it was built in 1974.

facts.fact: Facing Sakurada Street and Gaien-Higashi Street, it is known for its extensive brickwork and large entrance.
facts.quote: Facing Sakurada Street and Gaien-Higashi Street, the building is notable for its extensive use of brick stones and large entrance.

facts.fact: A red-brick base about 8 metres high carries an elliptical-cylinder upper part with almost no windows; the building houses the Embassy of Fiji.
facts.quote: It consists of a red-brick base of about 8 meters height and a copper sulfate shaped as an elliptical cylinder upper part with almost no windows (with only a full-length one on the 8th or 9th floor), and hosts the Embassy of Fiji.

facts.fact: It is 61.75 metres tall, with 15 floors above ground and 2 below.
facts.quote: It has a height of 61.75 meters, with 15 floors above and 2 below ground.

facts.fact: The real-estate founder Yoshitsuru Nagao gave the design to Shirai.
facts.quote: The design of the building was entrusted to Seiichi Shirai by founder Yoshitsuru Nagao, whose real estate corporation was founded in 1969.

facts.fact: Shirai's unusual use of materials rare in Japan, such as marble, brick and natural stone, sets his buildings apart from their surroundings.
facts.quote: His unexpected way of using exquisite and rare (in Japan) materials (marmor, brick, nature stone) make his buildings seem to be independent of their surrounding and at odds with the common Japanese architecture of this time.

facts.fact: Takanawa Gateway is a JR East station, the newest on the Yamanote and Keihin–Tōhoku lines and the only Yamanote station opened this century.
facts.quote: The station is operated by the East Japan Railway Company (JR East). It is the newest station on both the Yamanote and Keihin–Tōhoku Lines, and the only Yamanote Line station opened in the 21st century.

facts.fact: The station was designed by Kengo Kuma.
facts.quote: The station was designed by Kengo Kuma.

facts.fact: It has four tracks and two island platforms, with the concourse on the second floor.
facts.quote: Takanawa Gateway Station has 4 tracks and 2 island platforms. Each platform equipped 3 escalators, 1 24-person elevator and 1 18-person elevator to the paid area of the concourse on the second floor.

facts.fact: It was built above the existing Tamachi Depot, 13 hectares of which were redeveloped.
facts.quote: The station was built above the existing Tamachi Depot, with 13 hectares (32 acres) of the Depot's space being repurposed and redeveloped.

facts.fact: Construction began on 10 February 2017.
facts.quote: On 10 February 2017, construction on the station began.

facts.fact: The station opened on 14 March 2020.
facts.quote: The station opened on 14 March 2020, ten days before the summer Olympics were postponed to 2021 as a result of the COVID-19 pandemic.

facts.fact: The Kasumigaseki Building is a 36-storey skyscraper in Kasumigaseki, Tokyo.
facts.quote: The Kasumigaseki Building (霞が関ビルディング, Kasumigaseki birudingu) is a 36-story skyscraper located in Kasumigaseki, Chiyoda, Tokyo.

facts.fact: Completed in 1968, it is widely regarded as Japan's first modern office skyscraper.
facts.quote: Completed in 1968, the building is widely regarded as the first modern office skyscraper in Japan.

facts.fact: Taller buildings had not been possible because Japan's building law capped height at 31 metres until 1963.
facts.quote: The reason high-rise buildings were not built in the country earlier was that Japan's Building Standard Law set an absolute height limit of 31 meters (102 ft) until 1963, when the limit was abolished in favor of a Floor Area Ratio limit.

facts.fact: It is owned by the Kasumi Kaikan, an association of the former kazoku nobility.
facts.quote: The building is owned by the Kasumi Kaikan (霞会館), an association of the former kazoku high nobility.

facts.fact: Kajima Construction built it, and it was the subject of the film Chōkōsō no Akebono.
facts.quote: The Kasumigaseki Building is the main subject of the film Chōkōsō no Akebono, which was backed by Kajima Construction, the company that built the Kasumigaseki Building.

facts.fact: It became Japan's yardstick for comparing large volumes until the Tokyo Dome was built.
facts.quote: The building was often used for comparison to things with large volumes in Japan which continued until the construction of the Tokyo Dome, a huge indoor stadium.

facts.fact: The Nippon Budokan is an arena in Chiyoda, Tokyo, first built for judo at the 1964 Olympics.
facts.quote: The Nippon Budokan, often shortened to simply Budokan, is an arena in Chiyoda, Tokyo, originally built for Judo at the 1964 Summer Olympics.

facts.fact: Mamoru Yamada designed it among several structures linked to the 1964 Tokyo Olympics.
facts.quote: Later work included a number of structures associated with the 1964 Tokyo Olympics, including the Nippon Budokan (1964), Kyoto Tower (1964), as well as the Yamatokoriyama City Hall (1962)

facts.fact: The octagonal building is 42 metres high and holds 14,471 people.
facts.quote: The 42 metres (138 ft) high octagonal structure holds 14,471 people (arena seats: 2,946, first floor seats: 3,199, second floor seats: 7,846, standee: 480).

facts.fact: Built mainly for martial arts, it has also become famous as one of the world's great music venues.
facts.quote: While its primary purpose is to host martial arts contests, the arena has gained additional fame as one of the world's most outstanding musical performance venues.

facts.fact: The Beatles were the first rock group to play there, in 1966, against opposition from those who felt it would defile a martial arts hall.
facts.quote: The Beatles were the first rock group to play at the Budokan, in a series of five concerts, each lasting 30 minutes, June 30 – July 2, 1966. Their appearances were met with opposition from those who felt the appearance of a western pop group would defile the martial arts arena.

facts.fact: Kyoto Tower is a steel tower, the tallest structure in Kyoto, with its observation deck at 100 m and spire at 131 m, standing on a nine-storey building with a hotel and shops.
facts.quote: The steel tower is the tallest structure in Kyoto with its observation deck at 100 metres (328 ft) and its spire at 131 metres (430 ft). The 800-ton tower stands atop a 9-story building, which houses a 3-star hotel and several stores.

facts.fact: Instead of a lattice frame, its structure is made of steel rings stacked on top of each other.
facts.quote: Unlike many other towers (such as Tokyo Tower) that are constructed using metal lattice frames, Kyoto Tower's interior structure consists of many steel rings stacked on top of each other.

facts.fact: It is skinned in welded steel sheets 12–22 mm thick, painted white so the tower resembles a Japanese candle.
facts.quote: The structure was then covered with lightweight steel sheets with a thickness of 12–22 mm (0.47–0.87 in). The sheets were then welded together and painted white. The intended overall effect was for the tower to resemble a Japanese candle.

facts.fact: Mamoru Yamada designed it, with engineer Makoto Tanahashi, to withstand earthquakes and typhoons.
facts.quote: Designed by modernist architect, Mamoru Yamada with the expert advice of Makoto Tanahashi, a doctor of engineering at Kyoto University, Kyoto Tower was built to withstand the forces of both earthquakes and typhoons.

facts.fact: Construction began in 1963 on the former site of Kyoto's central post office and was completed near the end of 1964.
facts.quote: Construction began in 1963 on the former site of Kyoto's central post office and was completed near the end of 1964.

facts.fact: Many people opposed its cost and thought its needle-shaped spire too modern for the ancient capital.
facts.quote: Public opposition not only stemmed from the tower's ¥380 million ($1.056 million in 1963) price tag, but also from the fact that many believed the needle-shaped spire was too modern looking for the ancient capital.

facts.fact: A nine-storey building fully supports the 800-ton tower and gives it its first 30.8 metres of height.
facts.quote: The second structure that completely supports the 800-ton tower and gives it its first 30.8 meters of height is a nine-story building.

facts.fact: Kirjatalo is a commercial building in central Helsinki designed by Alvar Aalto, best known as the flagship store of the Academic Bookstore.
facts.quote: Kirjatalo (Swedish: Bokhuset; lit. 'Book House') is a commercial building located on the corner of Pohjoisesplanadi and Keskuskatu in central Helsinki, Finland. It is notable for having been designed by Alvar Aalto. Possibly its best-known resident is the flagship store of the Academic Bookstore chain.

facts.fact: Aalto won a 1961 competition held by the department store Stockmann, which owned the plot.
facts.quote: In 1961, the plot's owner, retail company Stockmann, whose main department store is located across the street, announced an architectural competition for the design of a new mixed-use property on the site. The winner of that contest was Alvar Aalto, who had also designed the nearby Rautatalo.

facts.fact: Its copper-clad exterior and central atrium were designed to match Aalto's nearby Rautatalo.
facts.quote: Both the copper-clad exterior, and the central atrium concept of the building's interior, were designed to match those of the Rautatalo.

facts.fact: The atrium is lit by skylights that extend down from the roof, with mezzanine floors around it.
facts.quote: The central space making up the atrium receives natural illumination from the skylights extending downwards from the roof. Surrounding the atrium are the upper floors' mezzanine structures.

facts.fact: The upper floors, first meant for offices, were later taken over by the bookshop.
facts.quote: The upper floors, originally allocated to office use, have subsequently been taken over by the book store.

facts.fact: Café Aalto opened on the first floor in 1986.
facts.quote: There is a restaurant, Café Aalto, opened in 1986, located on the first floor of the building.

facts.fact: Filmhuset in Gärdet, Stockholm, houses the Swedish Film Institute.
facts.quote: The institute is housed in the Filmhuset ("House of Film")  located in Gärdet, Östermalm, in Stockholm.

facts.fact: Peter Celsing designed it in the Brutalist style, and it was built between 1968 and 1971.
facts.quote: The building, completed in 1970, was designed in Brutalist style by architect Peter Celsing, and built between 1968 and 1971.

facts.fact: It was designed to look like a camera, with an exposed concrete facade that resembles film strips.
facts.quote: It was designed to resemble a camera, with an exposed concrete façade resembling filmstrips.

facts.fact: A major renovation in 2008 created open-plan offices.
facts.quote: It underwent a major renovation in 2008, creating open-plan offices.

facts.fact: Stockholm City Museum lists it 'code blue', its highest grade of cultural and historical value.
facts.quote: The building is listed as "code blue", the highest ranking in terms of cultural and historical value of buildings by the Stockholm City Museum (Stadsmuseet Stockholm).

facts.fact: It holds a large archive of books and magazines on film.
facts.quote: Filmhuset houses a large archive, containing books and magazines on film.

facts.fact: Henie Onstad Kunstsenter is an art museum on a headland in the Oslofjord at Høvikodden, about 10 km southwest of Oslo.
facts.quote: The Henie Onstad Kunstsenter is an art museum located at Høvikodden in Bærum municipality in Akershus county, Norway. It is situated on a headland jutting into the Oslofjord, approximately 10 kilometres (6.2 mi) southwest of Oslo.

facts.fact: It was founded in 1968 by figure skater Sonja Henie and her husband, shipowner and collector Niels Onstad.
facts.quote: The art center was founded in 1968 by World and Olympic champion figure skater Sonja Henie (1912–1969) and her husband, shipping magnate and art collector Niels Onstad (1909–1978).

facts.fact: Jon Eikvar and Svein-Erik Engebretsen won the 1964 design competition; it was their first commission.
facts.quote: In 1964, Sonja Henie and Niels Onstad announced an architectural competition for the art center. The competition was won by the Norwegian architects Jon Eikvar and Svein-Erik Engebretsen, and the project was their first architectural commission.

facts.fact: Completed in 1968, it was designed to fit the landscape along the fjord, using glass, stone, natural concrete and copper.
facts.quote: The art center was completed in 1968 and was designed to adapt to the landscape along the Oslo Fjord. The architecture uses materials such as glass, stone, natural concrete, and copper.

facts.fact: The same architects added a two-storey wing in 1994 as an organic extension of the main building.
facts.quote: This project was designed by the same architects—the new wing abuts the main body of the building as an organic extension.

facts.fact: Today it covers about 9,500 square metres, 3,500 of them exhibition space.
facts.quote: Today, the total building area is approximately 9,500 square meters, of which 3,500 are occupied by exhibition spaces.

facts.fact: A sculpture park with 30 sculptures surrounds the centre.
facts.quote: The art centre is surrounded by a sculpture park containing 30 sculptures.

facts.fact: Sanomatalo is a commercial and office building in central Helsinki, north of the Central railway station and south of the Helsinki Music Centre.
facts.quote: Sanomatalo (Swedish: Sanomahuset) is a commercial and office building in central Helsinki, Finland, to the north of Postitalo and the Helsinki Central railway station and to the south of the Helsinki Music Centre.

facts.fact: It has twelve floors, three of them underground.
facts.quote: It has twelve floors of which three are underground.

facts.fact: Designed by Jan Söderlund and Antti-Matti Siikala and completed in 1999, it was Helsinki's first glass building, and environmentalists protested that its glass walls might kill birds.
facts.quote: The building was designed by professor Jan Söderlund and architect Antti-Matti Siikala and it was completed in 1999. It was the first "glassy" building in Helsinki, and environmentalists protested against the glass walls because they might cause bird deaths.

facts.fact: It was also criticised for two extra floors built against the zoning plan.
facts.quote: There have also been protests against the building because it had two additional floors built contrary to the zoning plan.

facts.fact: Newspaper and radio offices fill open-plan floors at the top, while the two lower floors are commercial and exhibition space.
facts.quote: The offices of Helsingin Sanomat, Ilta-Sanomat, Taloussanomat, Radio Rock, Radio Suomipop, Loop, Helmiradio, HitMix, and Me Naiset Radio are located in open offices at the top floors of the building. The two lower floors are commercial and exhibition spaces: they include for example an R-kioski branch.

facts.fact: The Sibelius Hall is a concert hall in Lahti named after Jean Sibelius, completed in 2000.
facts.quote: The Sibelius Hall (Finnish: Sibeliustalo) is a concert hall in Lahti, Finland, named for the composer Jean Sibelius. The concert hall was completed in 2000.

facts.fact: Kimmo Lintula and Hannu Tikka designed the hall, built of glulam timber.
facts.quote: Architects Kimmo Lintula and Hannu Tikka designed the hall, which is made out of glulam.

facts.fact: Artec Consultants of New York engineered the acoustics, which are among the hall's strongest points.
facts.quote: The acoustics were engineered by Artec Consultants, New York. Its acoustics are one of its strongest points, while the architecture follows the Scandinavian tradition of sophisticated design.

facts.fact: The hall seats 1,250.
facts.quote: The concert hall has a capacity of 1,250 seats.

facts.fact: It is a large congress and concert centre and home of the Lahti Symphony Orchestra.
facts.quote: Lahti harbors cultural ambitions, manifested notably in the construction of a large congress and concert centre, the Sibelius Hall (2000) by architects Kimmo Lintula and Hannu Tikka. Lahti has one of Finland's most widely known symphony orchestras, the Lahti Symphony Orchestra (Sinfonia Lahti ), based at the Sibelius Hall, which performs both classical and popular music, notably concentrating on music by Jean Sibelius.

facts.fact: Stockholm City Hall stands on the eastern tip of Kungsholmen by Riddarfjärden; it holds offices and ceremonial halls and is the venue of the Nobel Prize banquet.
facts.quote: It stands on the eastern tip of Kungsholmen island, next to Riddarfjärden's northern shore and facing the islands of Riddarholmen and Södermalm. It houses offices and conference rooms as well as ceremonial halls. It is the venue of the Nobel Prize banquet and is one of Stockholm's major tourist attractions.

facts.fact: Ragnar Östberg won the commission after a competition and reworked his design, taking the tower from Carl Westman's entry.
facts.quote: After a further competition between Westman and Östberg, the latter was assigned the construction of the City Hall, while the former was asked to build Stockholm Court House. Östberg modified his original draft using elements of Westman's design, including the tower.

facts.fact: It took twelve years to build, from 1911 to 1923, using nearly eight million red bricks.
facts.quote: Construction took twelve years, from 1911 to 1923. Nearly eight million red bricks were used.

facts.fact: It is National Romantic, and its waterside site inspired the theme of city architecture set against water.
facts.quote: Stockholm City Hall is an example of National Romantic style. The site, overlooking Riddarfjärden, inspired a central motif, namely the juxtaposition of city architecture and water that represents a central feature of Stockholm's cityscape as a whole.

facts.fact: The style blends austere Northern European brick with Venetian Gothic touches such as turrets, balconies and statues.
facts.quote: The hall's style is one of refined eclecticism, blending massive, austere, Northern European brick construction with whimsical elements reminiscent of Venetian Gothic architecture, such as turrets adorned with golden starlets, decorated balconies, wooden masts, and statues.

facts.fact: The Blue Hall is treated like a formal courtyard and has no blue decoration; the name comes from Östberg's first draft.
facts.quote: The Blue Hall (Blå hallen), with its straight walls and arcades, incorporates elements of a formal courtyard. Its walls are in fact without blue decorations; the name derives from Östberg's first draft, and is notable as the dining hall where banquets are held after the annual Nobel Prize award ceremony.

facts.fact: The 106-metre tower at the waterside corner is topped by the Three Crowns, Sweden's national symbol.
facts.quote: The southeast corner of the building, immediately adjacent to the shore, is dominated by a monumental tower topped with the Three Crowns, the Swedish national symbol. The tower is 106 metres high and is accessible by lift or a 365 step staircase.

facts.fact: The 44-metre Golden Hall is named after the mosaics by Einar Forseth that decorate its walls, proposed by Östberg.
facts.quote: Measuring 44-metre (144 ft) in length, it received its name when its walls were decorated by mosaics created by the artist Einar Forseth on a proposal by the City Hall architect Ragnar Östberg.

facts.fact: The Helsinki Olympic Stadium, in Töölö about 2.3 km from the city centre, is Finland's largest stadium and was the centre of the 1952 Olympics.
facts.quote: The Helsinki Olympic Stadium (Finnish: Helsingin Olympiastadion; Swedish: Helsingfors Olympiastadion), located in the Töölö district about 2.3 kilometres (1.4 mi) from the centre of the Finnish capital Helsinki, is the largest stadium in the country. The stadium is best known for being the centre of activities in the 1952 Summer Olympics.

facts.fact: It was designed by Yrjö Lindegren and Toivo Jäntti and is known as an icon of functionalist architecture.
facts.quote: The Olympic Stadium was designed by the architects Yrjö Lindegren and Toivo Jäntti. The Olympic stadium, known as an icon of functionalist style of architecture, was featured in the Architectural Digest as one of the best examples of Olympic architecture.

facts.fact: Built from 1934 to 1938 for the 1940 Games, which were cancelled because of the Second World War, it hosted the 1952 Olympics instead.
facts.quote: Construction of the Olympic Stadium began in 1934 and it was completed in 1938, with the intent to host the 1940 Summer Olympics, which were moved from Tokyo to Helsinki before being cancelled due to World War II. It hosted the 1952 Summer Olympics over a decade later instead.

facts.fact: The 72.71-metre tower measures the length of Matti Järvinen's gold-medal javelin throw at the 1932 Olympics.
facts.quote: The tower of the stadium, a distinct landmark with a height of 72.71 metres (238.5 ft), a measurement of the length of the gold-medal win by Matti Järvinen in javelin throw of 1932 Summer Olympics.

facts.fact: It held over 70,000 people in 1952 with temporary upper tiers; today it seats 36,251.
facts.quote: The stadium's spectator capacity was at its maximum during the 1952 Summer Olympics with over 70,000 spectator places (this capacity was achieved by temporarily extending its upper tier on its north, east and south stands). Nowadays the stadium has 36,251 spectator places.

facts.fact: A renovation begun in 2016 covered all the stands with canopies; the stadium reopened in 2020.
facts.quote: During renovation all the spectator stands were covered with canopies and the field area and the tracks were renewed. The stadium now also offers extended restaurant areas and more indoor sport venues. The renovation was completed and the stadium was open to the public in September 2020.

facts.fact: Lindegren himself won the Olympic gold medal for town planning at the 1948 London Games.
facts.quote: He won the Olympic gold medal in the town planning category of architecture at the 1948 Summer Olympics in London.

facts.fact: Sven Markelius began work on the Helsingborg Concert Hall in 1932, among his major civic projects.
facts.quote: Meanwhile, among his major civic projects, Markelius began work on the Concert Hall in Helsingborg in 1932.

facts.fact: The hall was completed in 1934.
facts.quote: 1932 - Helsingborg Concert Hall (completed 1934)

facts.fact: It is listed among the notable buildings completed in 1934.
facts.quote: Helsingborg Concert Hall, designed by Sven Markelius.

facts.fact: The Bank of Sweden building at Brunkebergstorg in Stockholm was one of Peter Celsing's last buildings; its design is ruled by cubes, squares, spheres and circles meant to suggest stability.
facts.quote: One of his last buildings is the Bank of Sweden (Sveriges Riksbank) building at Brunkebergstorg in Stockholm, the design of which is dominated by the use of cubes, squares, spheres and circles, all intended to give the impression of stability.

facts.fact: Its facade uses thick slabs of rough-hewn dark granite, borrowing the Renaissance and neo-Renaissance use of rustication on bank buildings to look solid.
facts.quote: It makes use of thick slabs of roughly hewn dark granite in the façade, thus borrowing from the Renaissance tradition of using rustication to give the impression of solidity and particularly from the 19th century neo-Renaissance practice of using rustication in bank buildings for this purpose.

facts.fact: The bank moved into Celsing's building in 1976 from its semi-circular home on Helgeandsholmen.
facts.quote: The Bank of Sweden had since 1907 been located to a semi-circular building on Helgeandsholmen, but moved to Celsing's building in 1976.

facts.fact: Built 1969–1973, it stands next to Celsing's Kulturhuset and is among his best-known works.
facts.quote: The best-known examples of this are the Kulturhuset (House of Culture) at Sergels torg in central Stockholm (1966–1971), the adjacent headquarters of the Bank of Sweden (1969–1973), and his addition to Carolina Rediviva, the main building of the Uppsala University Library (1953–1962).

facts.fact: Celsing often worked in a brutalist manner with large exposed grey concrete surfaces, sometimes combined with large glass panes and wooden interior details.
facts.quote: Celsing often worked in a brutalist style with large exposed grey concrete surfaces, but occasionally combined this with large glass panes exposing the structure of the building from the outside, and interior details in wood.
